## DEUTERONOMY 22 — VERSE-BY-VERSE COMMENTARY NOTES

### OVERVIEW

Keil and Delitzsch (Lutheran) title this section: "The Duty to Love One's Neighbour; and Warning Against a Violation of the Natural Order of Things. Instructions to Sanctify the Marriage State." J. Vernon McGee notes that chapters 22–26 shift from national regulations to "domestic and personal relations"—laws for where the people actually live.[¹] Meredith Kline (Reformed) sees the unifying theme as "Sanctity of the Divine Order"—love for God requires reverence for divine ordinances in nature (vv.5–12), marriage (vv.13–30), and the theocratic kingdom.[²]

---

### vv. 1–4: Kindness to a Neighbor's Property

**v. 1:** "You must not ignore it; be sure to return it to your brother." The Hebrew literally means "hide yourself"—do not pretend you did not see. David Guzik (Enduring Word, charismatic-evangelical) says God here condemns the sin of doing nothing: "To see your brother in need, and to do nothing, is to do evil." G. Campbell Morgan adds, "We are not only responsible that we do no harm to our fellow-men; we are also responsible to prevent harm."[³] John Gill (Baptist, 18th c.) notes that "brother" here is not limited to kin or even fellow Israelites—Exodus 23:4 extends the same duty to enemies, so this is "a piece of humanity the law of nature requires."[⁴]

— [³] https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-22/
— [⁴] https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/22.htm

**v. 2:** If the owner is distant or unknown, the finder must keep the animal at home until the owner seeks it. Precept Austin calls this "Finder's Keepers with an Asterisk"—the principle is the opposite of the children's rhyme: you keep it only to protect it for the owner. Gill notes that the Jewish Mishnah (Bava Metzia) set specific holding times: twelve months for large cattle, three months for smaller, and required public proclamation.[⁵] Jack Deere (The Bible Knowledge Commentary) observes that the regulation targets "the natural tendency to ignore it because of the extra time and labor involved in restoring it."[⁶]

— [⁵] https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/22.htm
— [⁶] https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-22-commentary

**v. 3:** The principle extends beyond animals to "anything your brother has lost." Precept Austin notes this would today include purses, wallets, keys, credit cards, jewelry, papers—anything found must be returned. The repeated refrain "you must not hide yourself" (vv.1, 3, 4) is the key phrase: deliberate neglect is tantamount to stealing.[⁷]

— [⁷] https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-22-commentary

**v. 4:** The fallen animal must be helped up—even if it belongs to an enemy (Exodus 23:4–5). Precept Austin quotes J. Vernon McGee: "They were not to assume a nonchalant attitude … nor pass by as if the neighbor's problem were none of their business."[⁸] Guzik notes that Jesus' parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:31–32) is a commentary on this principle. Brown (The Message of Deuteronomy) applies it to modern social evils: Christians must not "hide themselves" from problems like abortion, pornography, homelessness, and drug abuse.[⁹]

— [⁸] https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-22-commentary
— [⁹] https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-22-commentary

---

### v. 5: Prohibition of Cross-Dressing

**Traditional reading:** All major Protestant traditions agree this verse upholds the created distinction between male and female (Genesis 1:27) and forbids deliberately blurring that line through clothing.

**The word "pertains" (Hebrew *keli*):** The Pulpit Commentary notes it literally means the "apparatus" of a man—including not only dress but implements, tools, weapons, and utensils. It is "an ethical regulation in the interests of morality. … Whatever tends to obliterate the distinction between the sexes tends to licentiousness."[¹⁰] Keil and Delitzsch (Lutheran) explain: "The immediate design of this prohibition was not to prevent licentiousness, or to oppose idolatrous practices … but to maintain the sanctity of that distinction of the sexes which was established by the creation of man and woman."[¹¹]

— [¹⁰] https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/22.htm
— [¹¹] https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/22-12.html (Keil & Delitzsch citation)

**John Calvin (Reformed):** "Garments are not in themselves of so much importance; but as it is disgraceful for men to become effeminate, and also for women to affect manliness in their dress and gestures, propriety and modesty are prescribed … lest one kind of liberty should at length lead to something worse." Calvin quotes a heathen poet approvingly and says, "Decency in the fashion of the clothes is an excellent preservative of modesty."[¹²]

— [¹²] https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/deuteronomy-22.html

**John Gill (Baptist):** Gill notes that the law opposes effeminacy in men and immodesty in women, and suggests a connection to pagan idolatrous customs—citing Maimonides, who reported that in the Zabian cult men wore women's coloured garments before Venus and women wore armour before Mars. Gill adds that the precept is "agreeably to the law and light of nature," citing a classical writer who called cross-dressing part of the unwritten natural law.[¹³]

— [¹³] https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/22.htm

**Matthew Henry (Puritan/Reformed):** Henry sees two applications: (1) it forbids the idolatrous custom of Gentiles, where "in the worship of Venus, women appeared in armour, and men in women's clothes"; (2) it forbids "the confounding of the dispositions and affairs of the sexes: men must not be effeminate … nor must women be viragos, pretend to teach, or usurp authority (1 Timothy 2:11–12)."[¹⁴]

— [¹⁴] https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/22-12.html (Matthew Henry citation)

**David Guzik (Enduring Word, charismatic-evangelical):** Guzik is explicit that "this is not a command against women wearing a garment that in some ways might be common between men and women. A woman can wear trousers without looking like a man. It is a command against dressing in a manner which deliberately crosses or blurs the distinction between the sexes." He calls the rise of cross-dressing, transvestitism, and transgender behavior "a shocking trampling of this command" that "will continue to reap a bitter harvest in more perversion and more gender confusion."[¹⁵]

— [¹⁵] https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-22/

**Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary:** "The modern 'uni-sex' look and 'liberated society' are evidence of a declining morality which is contrary to God’s righteous principles." Notes that "orderly societies of all ages and countries have clear-cut distinctions between the sexes."[¹⁶]

— [¹⁶] https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/deuteronomy-22.html

**Lutheran view (Keil & Delitzsch):** "Every violation or wiping out of this distinction—such even, for example, as the emancipation of a woman—was unnatural, and therefore an abomination in the sight of God."[¹⁷]

— [¹⁷] https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/22-12.html

**Key point of agreement across traditions:** All surveyed traditions (Baptist, Reformed, Lutheran, Puritan, charismatic-evangelical) treat this as a creation-order principle, not merely a culturally-bound ceremonial law. The practical question—whether women may wear trousers—is addressed by Guzik as a misapplication (trousers ≠ dressing like a man), but some Christian groups do apply it more strictly.

**Where I could not find material:** Catholic (newadvent.org, catholic.com), Orthodox (oca.org), Methodist (seedbed.com, wesley.nnu.edu), Pentecostal distinctives (pneumareview.com, ag.org), modern scholarship (bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org).

---

### vv. 6–7: The Bird's Nest Law

**v. 6:** "You must not take the mother along with the young." The Pulpit Commentary says these precepts "are designed to foster humane feeling towards the lower animals, and not less to preserve regard to that affectionate relation between parents and their young which God has established as a law in the animal world."[¹⁸] John Gill notes that the Jewish Mishnah (Cholin 12) specifies this applies only to wild clean birds, not domestic fowl, and requires letting the mother go even if she returns repeatedly—"even a thousand times," says Maimonides.[¹⁹]

— [¹⁸] https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/22.htm
— [¹⁹] https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/22.htm

**v. 7:** "So that it may be well with you and that you may prolong your days." Both Gill and the Pulpit Commentary note that this is the same blessing promised to those who honour father and mother (Deuteronomy 5:16)—one of the weightiest commands. Gill comments that some Jewish commentators regarded this as the smallest of all the commandments, yet God attached the same reward, showing that "God, in bestowing such rewards, has regard not to the works of men, but to his own grace and kindness."[²⁰] Matthew Poole (Puritan) says the law restrains "greediness and covetousness, that they should not monopolize all to themselves, but might leave the hopes of a future seed for others."[²¹] Thompson speculates: "Perhaps reverence for motherhood in general gave rise to the law."[²²]

— [²⁰] https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/22.htm
— [²¹] https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-22/ (Poole cited within)
— [²²] https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-22/ (Thompson cited within)

---

### v. 8: The Parapet (Railing) on the Roof

Since Israelite houses had flat roofs used for sleeping, conversation, and daily activities (cf. 1 Samuel 9:25–26; 2 Samuel 11:2), a railing was required to prevent fatal falls. The Pulpit Commentary: "Still less was human life to be exposed to danger through neglect of proper precautions."[²³] Charles Spurgeon (Baptist) preached a sermon titled "Battlements" on this text, applying it spiritually: "This careful command clearly shows us that God holds life to be very valuable, and … as he would not permit us to kill by malice, so he would not allow us to kill by negligence." Spurgeon extended the principle to "spiritual railings" that protect against sin: "It is of little use to go on till you are over the edge of the roof, and then cry, 'Halt.'"[²⁴] John Gill notes the Talmud extended the principle to any dangerous feature on one's property (a well must have a cover or fence).[²⁵]

— [²³] https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/22.htm
— [²⁴] https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-22/ (Spurgeon cited within)
— [²⁵] https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/22.htm

### vv. 9–11: Three Laws Against Mixing

**v. 9: Mixed seed in a vineyard.** **v. 10: Plowing with ox and donkey together.** **v. 11: Wool and linen woven together.**

**The traditional reading (most Protestant teachers):** These laws were primarily designed to separate Israel from pagan, occult customs. Adam Clarke (Methodist, cited by Guzik): "It is generally supposed that mixtures of different sorts in seed, breed, etc., were employed for superstitious purposes, and therefore prohibited."[²⁶] The Pulpit Commentary offers a slightly different emphasis: "God has made distinctions in nature, and these are not to be confounded by the mixing of things distinct. The ox and the ass were chiefly used in husbandry; but, as they were of different size and strength, it was not only fitting that they should not be yoked to the same plough, but it might be cruel so to yoke them."[²⁷]

— [²⁶] https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-22/
— [²⁷] https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/22.htm

**Spiritual application:** David Guzik connects the command against unequal yoking to Paul's principle in 2 Corinthians 6:14: "Do not be unequally yoked together with unbelievers." Matthew Poole (Puritan) says these laws, "though in themselves small and trivial, are given … to forbid all mixture of their inventions with God's institutions, in doctrine or worship."[²⁸] Warren Wiersbe (evangelical): "The Bible makes it clear that 'God is not the author of confusion' (1 Cor. 14:33), but confusion results when we ignore the distinctions God has made."[²⁹]

— [²⁸] https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-22/
— [²⁹] https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-22-commentary (Wiersbe cited within)

**An unusual view:** Jamieson-Fausset-Brown suggests that the prohibition on yoking ox and donkey together was partly because "the ass, from feeding on coarse and poisonous weed, has a fetid breath, which its yoke-fellow seeks to avoid, not only as poisonous and offensive, but producing leanness, or, if long continued, death."[³⁰]

— [³⁰] https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-22/ (JFB cited within)

---

### v. 12: Tassels on Garments

This command is explained in Numbers 15:37–41: the tassels (*tzitzit*) were a reminder to Israel to keep God's commandments. Thompson notes: "A symbolic meaning is given to these tassels … namely that they are a reminder to Israel to keep God's law."[³¹] Guzik adds that the tassels also distinguished an Israelite man from his pagan neighbors. In Jesus' day, the Pharisees "enlarge the borders of their garments" (Matthew 23:5)—making tassels prominent to show off their piety, corrupting a good command.[³²]

— [³¹] https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-22/
— [³²] https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-22/

---

### vv. 13–21: Accusation Against a Bride's Virginity

**v. 13:** The case: a man marries, consummates the marriage, then comes to hate his wife. Ellicott's Commentary notes the parallel in 2 Samuel 13:15, where Amnon hated Tamar after violating her—sated lust turning to loathing.[³³]

— [³³] https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/22.htm

**vv. 14–15:** The husband accuses her of not being a virgin. The parents produce "the cloth"—a bloodstained garment from the wedding night, kept as evidence. Guzik notes this custom "is still practiced among some peoples today," and Kalland adds, "The proofs of virginity, the blood-spotted bedclothes or garments, which, though not infallible, were widely accepted in the ancient Near East as indications of prior virginity, are still accepted among some peoples today."[³⁴]

— [³⁴] https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-22/

**vv. 18–19:** If the accusation is false, the man is punished, fined 100 shekels of silver (paid to the bride's father), and permanently forfeits the right to divorce her. Merrill notes that David bought Araunah's threshing floor and oxen for only 50 shekels (2 Samuel 24:24)—so 100 shekels "was considerable relative to that economy" and "would clearly deter young husbands from such frivolous and fallacious allegations."[³⁵] Gill adds that the slander was considered "a kind of murder" (cf. Ezekiel 22:9).[³⁶]

— [³⁵] https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-22/
— [³⁶] https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/22.htm

**vv. 20–21:** If the accusation is true, the woman is stoned at the door of her father's house. Gill explains this was the death for adulteresses of this sort (betrothed but not yet taken to the husband's house); other forms of adultery were by strangling, and a priest's daughter was to be burned (Leviticus 20:10; 21:9). The phrase "she hath wrought folly in Israel" first appears in Genesis 34:7 (after the naming of Israel) and "entailed a higher standard of behaviour upon Jacob's family," per Ellicott.[³⁷] Guzik notes that this law must be read alongside Exodus 22:16–17, which protects a seduced virgin: the woman in this case was "truly wanton"—she had given up her virginity but did not claim her rights under Exodus 22 and instead deceived her husband.[³⁸]

— [³⁷] https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/22.htm
— [³⁸] https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-22/

---

### v. 22: The Penalty for Adultery

Both the man and the woman must die. Gill notes this mirrors Leviticus 20:10; the Targum of Jonathan specifies death by strangling. Guzik stresses that the death penalty "applied equally to both man and woman, with no double standard." However, Guzik adds that in practice it was rarely carried out because any capital crime required two or three eyewitnesses willing to initiate the execution (Deuteronomy 17:6–7)—and in adultery cases, such witnesses would almost never be available.[³⁹] This background helps explain the scene in John 8:1–12, where Jesus confronts those who brought the woman taken in adultery but not the man. Ellicott notes that Jesus did not dispute the law itself: "Moses in the Law commanded us that such should be stoned" (John 8:5).[⁴⁰]

— [³⁹] https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-22/
— [⁴⁰] https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/22.htm

---

### vv. 23–27: The Betrothed Virgin — City vs. Country

These laws distinguish between a betrothed woman (legally considered a wife; Ellicott notes she is called "his neighbour's wife" in v.24) assaulted in a city versus in the countryside.

**vv. 23–24 (in the city):** Both are stoned—the woman because she did not cry out (her silence implies consent), the man because he violated his neighbour's wife. Gill explains that being in the city, her cry could have been heard, and as a betrothed woman she "ought to have abode in her father's house till her husband fetched her home, and not to have gadded abroad in the city."[⁴¹]

— [⁴¹] https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/22.htm

**vv. 25–27 (in the open country):** Only the man dies. The woman is presumed innocent because even if she cried out, no one could hear. Guzik: "The law protected women while holding them responsible only when truly culpable."[⁴²] Verse 26 explicitly compares it to murder: "just as when a man attacks his neighbor and murders him."

— [⁴²] https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-22/

---

### vv. 28–29: Seduction of an Unbetrothed Virgin

If a man seizes and lies with a virgin who is not betrothed, he must pay her father 50 shekels of silver, marry her, and may never divorce her. Ellicott notes that Exodus 22:16–17 provides the parallel: the father could refuse the marriage, but the seducer must still pay the bride-price.[⁴³] Gill and the Bible.org commentary note that a father might be too poor to have his daughter engaged, or the girl might be mentally incapacitated—in such cases the law ensured her protection. Gill says the prohibition on divorce "was wisely ordered to preserve chastity."[⁴⁴]

— [⁴³] https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/22.htm
— [⁴⁴] https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/22.htm

---

### v. 30 (Hebrew Bible 23:1): Prohibition on Marrying a Father's Wife

This forbids a son from marrying (or lying with) his father's wife—whether his own mother or a stepmother. Gill notes Aben Ezra extends it to "anyone that was deflowered by his father," and Jarchi interprets it as including a father's brother's wife (the levirate marriage exception in Deuteronomy 25:5). Gill calls this verse "a short memorandum" to remind Israel of all the incest laws in Leviticus 18.[⁴⁵] Ellicott concurs: "A principle, not merely a precept, is implied here, as appears by the details of Leviticus 18."[⁴⁶] The phrase "uncover his father's skirt" (KJV) means to violate the marriage relationship the father had established.

— [⁴⁵] https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/22.htm
— [⁴⁶] https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/22.htm

---

### WHERE PROTESTANT TRADITIONS DIFFER

**v. 5 (cross-dressing):** The traditions surveyed largely agree on the principle—maintaining the creation-order distinction between male and female. The difference is one of emphasis and application:
- **Reformed/Calvin:** Emphasizes modesty and decency, with Calvin saying garments themselves are not the core issue but the "disgraceful" effeminacy or manliness they signal.
- **Lutheran (Keil & Delitzsch):** Rooted in the created order; even "the emancipation of a woman" was seen as a violation.
- **Baptist (Gill, Garner-Howes):** Generally applies it to gender confusion and links it to pagan idolatry, but also to natural law.
- **Charismatic/Evangelical (Guzik):** Explicitly rejects the "women can't wear pants" interpretation; focuses on deliberate blurring of gender lines and contemporary transgender issues.

**vv. 9–11 (mixing laws):** Most traditions see these as ceremonial/symbolic pointing to spiritual separation. The Pulpit Commentary adds a practical animal-welfare dimension to v.10 (the unequal yoke would be cruel to both animals). No sharp doctrinal disagreement found among the sources.
